questions.q: What is a GitHub Issue typically used for, as distinct from a pull request?
options: Tracking a bug report, feature request, task, or question — the work before a specific code change exists, unlike a PR which proposes an actual change
Issues and pull requests are exactly the same thing
Issues are only for reporting problems with GitHub itself, not a project's own code
Issues automatically write the code needed to fix them
questions.explain: Issues are GitHub's lightweight tracker for work items; a pull request is the specific code change that (often) resolves one.

questions.q: What makes an issue like "expected the export button to download a CSV; instead it throws a 500 error, reproducible by clicking Export on any report with zero rows" more useful than "export is broken"?
options: It's written in a bigger font
It's specific: what was expected, what actually happened, and how to reproduce it, so no one has to guess
There's no real difference between the two
It automatically assigns itself to the right person
questions.explain: A specific, reproducible issue saves everyone — including the reporter, revisiting it later — from guessing what actually happened.

questions.q: What does a GitHub Project (board) typically organize?
options: Only billing and subscription information
A list of repository collaborators only
Nothing — Projects are purely decorative
Issues and pull requests, usually in columns like Backlog, In Progress, and Done
questions.explain: Project boards give a visual, column-based view built from a repository's (or organization's) issues and PRs.

questions.q: What happens when a pull request's description contains the phrase `Closes #42`?
options: Nothing — this phrase has no special meaning to GitHub
It deletes issue #42 immediately, without any code change
It links the PR to issue #42, and merging the PR automatically closes that issue
It prevents the PR from ever being merged
questions.explain: Closes/Fixes #<number> is GitHub's syntax for linking a PR to an issue and auto-closing it on merge.

questions.q: What completes at the end of this lesson, according to the course structure?
options: The entire course
Chapter 2, GitHub Essentials — the foundation (Git Fundamentals plus GitHub Essentials) the rest of the course builds on
Nothing — this is the first lesson of the course
Only the Capstone chapter
questions.explain: Lesson 11 is the last lesson of Chapter 2, completing the course's foundational two chapters.
